v.why: Obvious story says two parallel convs into the output compound, but saturation means the first 3x3 conv into node 3 already captures most of the gain, so the second adds less.
One might expect more capacity always to help equally, but a parent already containing the strongest op on the other output edge has little headroom left.
Deepening the chain looks like it should synergize with a conv on edge 5, but parents with a 3x3 conv on edge 5 are already near the ceiling, so gains shrink.
A conv on edge 0 might seem to feed a richer node 2 when edge 1 is also a conv, but redundant conv capacity saturates and leaves less room for improvement.
Adding a conv anywhere looks uniformly beneficial, but parents with a strong conv already on an output edge have reduced headroom.
Cutting an output edge looks catastrophic in strong cells, but when edge 4 carries a 3x3 conv the remaining path substitutes, so the loss is smaller.
Removing edge 4 seems to hurt strong cells most, but a 3x3 conv on edge 5 provides a redundant strong route, cushioning the removal.
A residual skip might be expected to protect against a weak op, but skip-equipped parents are stronger, so the harmful pooling edit loses more from a higher baseline.
The conv on edge 5 seems to compensate, but strong parents have more to lose, while weak parents sit near the floor where pooling looks harmless.
Removing the input-output edge seems irrelevant when a conv path exists, but strong conv-chain parents depend on it for trainability and have more accuracy to lose.
Cutting edge 0 removes node 1's input, but a 3x3 conv on edge 1 keeps a strong route through node 2, so the cost is smaller.
A cheap conv might seem to complement a 3x3 conv, but parents already holding the strongest op leave little headroom for a weaker conv.
Adding depth before a strong conv seems synergistic, but headroom limits gains in parents already strong at the output.
A downstream conv might seem to repair pooled features, but harmful edits cost more in strong parents than in weak ones near the floor.
The conv on edge 4 looks like it should absorb the damage, but it makes the parent strong, and harmful edits bite harder in strong parents.
When the conv replaces avg_pool, the edit swaps the weakest active op for the strongest, giving a bigger gain than replacing skip or 1x1 conv, and no gain when the edge was already conv3x3.
Filling an empty output edge with the strongest op adds both a path and capacity, so the gain exceeds that of replacing an existing op.
Deleting edge 5 costs most when it removes the strongest op rather than a weak pooling or an already-empty edge.
A strong conv elsewhere might seem to make edge 3 irrelevant, but in strong parents replacing the residual with pooling degrades more than in weak floor-level parents.
Pooling on the internal edge seems harmless when the output has a strong conv, but floor effects make harmful edits look benign only in weak parents, so strong parents lose more.

raw:
These hypotheses come from known structure in NAS-Bench-201, not from a fresh analysis of the benchmark table:

- nor_conv_3x3 is the dominant operation.
- Edges 4 and 5 feed the output and matter most.
- Edge 3 (skip from the input to the output) acts as a residual path.
- avg_pool_3x3 and none on output-feeding edges are usually harmful.

The conditions mostly require a nor_conv_3x3 on a key edge or a skip on edge 3, so many parents satisfy them. The set mixes saturation (a second strong op adds less), headroom (helpful edits gain less in strong parents), floor effects (harmful edits hurt more in strong parents), redundancy (removal costs less when a substitute exists) and replacement-identity conditions.
